q: A team is drawing a DFD for an LLM assistant and labels the model output as “trusted, because our system generates it.” Documents sent by customers also go into the context. What is the mistake?
options: The model output should be labeled secret, not trusted
Customer documents should not be drawn on the DFD
Trust propagates through the model: the output is as trusted as the least trusted input in the context, so here it is untrusted
The LLM process should be labeled as a trust boundary that cleans data
explain: The model does not “clean” input: if untrusted content enters the context, the output carries its influence. That is why output is treated as untrusted data (boundary B). Customer documents are exactly boundary C, which should be drawn.

q: At the workshop nobody drew the log platform to which the application sends full prompts and responses. Why is this an important omission?
options: Logs often contain personal data and secrets, and the log platform has a wider access circle than the application, so it is a flow through which information can leak
Logs affect the quality of the model's answers
The log platform is part of the vendor's model
Logs should never be kept, so there is no point in drawing them
explain: Telemetry is a data flow like any other and is often forgotten. Prompts and responses in logs carry sensitive data, and access to the log platform is usually broader. Logs are still needed (repudiation, IR), so they should be drawn and protected, not abolished.

q: Which combination of agent capabilities makes up the “lethal trifecta”?
options: A large model, a long context and a low temperature
Internet access, GPU and memory
Multiple agents, memory and RAG
Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally
explain: The lethal trifecta (Simon Willison) is the combination of private data, untrusted content and an outbound channel. Then indirect prompt injection can lead to data exfiltration. The defense is removing at least one of the three capabilities for a given flow.

q: An agent reads incoming emails (untrusted input), has access to a CRM with customer data and can send email. What does the Agents Rule of Two recommend?
options: Nothing, the rule only applies to agents with memory
The agent has all three properties (A, B, C), so it must not operate autonomously: it needs human confirmation or another reliable validation, separation of components or a new session
It is enough to add to the system prompt that it must not send data outside
Replace the model with a larger one because it is more resistant to injection
explain: The Rule of Two says an agent in a session should have at most two of three properties (untrusted input, access to sensitive data, state change/external communication). When all three are needed, oversight or a redesign is required. A prompt instruction and a larger model are not reliable controls.

q: How should a threat be recorded in a threat model for an AI system?
options: As an abuse case: actor, boundary, precondition, consequence, mapping to OWASP/ATLAS and controls
As the exact attack text the red team used
Only as an OWASP label, e.g., “LLM01”
As a CVSS score without a description
explain: An abuse case describes conditions and consequences that stay the same even when specific techniques change, and it leads directly to controls. A concrete payload quickly goes stale and is not needed for the decision. A label or score alone doesn't say what needs to be done.

q: Two agents use the same model and the same knowledge base. The first has a tool only for reading tickets, the second a tool for issuing refunds. What determines the difference in risk the most?
options: The size of the system prompt
The number of users who use the agent
Boundary D (actions): the consequence of a successful manipulation is completely different
The model's temperature
explain: In AI systems, impact is determined mostly by the actions the system can perform. The same model and the same likelihood of manipulation yield completely different risk depending on whether the tool only reads or triggers a financial transaction.

q: The only control for the threat “the agent sends internal data outside” is the sentence in the system prompt “never send data outside the company.” How should it be recorded in the register?
options: As closed, because a control exists
As an accepted risk, because the vendor's model is secure
As low likelihood, because models mostly follow instructions
As effectively uncontrolled (open) until an architectural or deterministic control is introduced
explain: A prompt instruction is probabilistic and can be bypassed. A high-impact threat needs a control that doesn't depend on the model: a recipient allowlist, user confirmation, removing the tool.

q: What is the correct order of control strength, from strongest to weakest, when choosing a response to a high-impact threat?
options: Guardrail model → prompt instruction → allowlist → privilege separation
Architectural (separation, removing tools) → deterministic checks in code → probabilistic classifiers
Probabilistic classifiers → architectural → deterministic
All controls are equally strong if they are documented
explain: Architectural controls remove the capability, deterministic checks in code enforce it reliably, and probabilistic filters reduce likelihood but can be bypassed. That is why filters are an additional layer, not the only control.

q: Match the example AI system threat with the STRIDE category.
options: There is no record of which retrieval and which prompt led to an agent action
An agent with a service account's permissions performs an action the user is not allowed to
A poisoned document in the RAG corpus changes the answers
The agent enters a loop of tool calls and exhausts the quota
explain: Missing traces is repudiation, an action beyond the user's permissions is elevation of privilege, modifying the corpus is tampering, and exhausting quotas is denial of service. Spoofing is a distractor.

q: The assistant needs to email a customer. The design proposes that the model extract the recipient address from the ticket text. Which design change reduces risk the most?
options: Add a filter that looks for suspicious words in the ticket
Increase the context window so the model understands the ticket better
Take the address from the customer record in the ticketing system, not from the model, with a review before sending
Log all sent emails
explain: When a high-impact parameter (the recipient) comes from a trusted source instead of the model, an entire class of risk disappears. A filter is probabilistic, logging is only detective, and a larger context doesn't affect the risk.

q: Which of the following events does NOT necessarily require a review of the agent's threat model?
options: Adding a tool for deleting records
A new document source in the RAG index
Switching to another vendor's model
Changing the color of a button in the user interface
explain: New tools, new data sources and a change of model or vendor change flows and boundaries, so they are review triggers. A cosmetic UI change doesn't change data flows or permissions.

q: A team wants its threat model not to go stale. What is the most effective mechanism?
options: Keep the threat model as code in the repo and have CI require an update to it when tools, data sources or model configuration change
Hold a workshop once a year
Send a PDF to all developers
Make the model vendor responsible for maintaining it
explain: A threat model as code goes through review together with changes, and a CI rule tied to key files (tools, sources, model) automatically prompts a review. An annual workshop is too slow for agents and RAG, which change quickly.

q: How do OWASP and ATLAS fit with STRIDE when threat modeling an AI system?
options: They replace STRIDE because STRIDE is outdated
STRIDE provides structure by elements and boundaries, while OWASP and ATLAS provide concrete AI threats that would otherwise be missed
They are used only after an incident
OWASP is used for training, and ATLAS only for serving
explain: STRIDE is generic and gives a systematic walkthrough, while the AI lists add specific threats (indirect injection, corpus poisoning, tool misuse). Neither list replaces the other.

q: An organization fine-tunes a model on a CI runner that has access to production secrets, and it downloads the base model from a public hub. Which DFD boundary is most critical for this flow?
options: Boundary E (supply chain): an external artifact is loaded into an environment with secrets
Boundary A (user → application)
Boundary B (model output → UI)
None, because the pipeline is not part of the application
explain: Loading an external artifact into an environment with production secrets is a classic supply chain issue (LLM03, AML.T0010). Controls: approved sources, safe formats, an isolated runner without production secrets, signatures. The pipeline is part of the system and gets drawn.

q: Assessing the likelihood of indirect prompt injection for an assistant that summarizes emails from anyone. Which approach is correct?
options: Low, until the red team proves exploitation
It depends on the size of the model
High as soon as boundary C (untrusted content in the context) exists; treat it as an assumption
Zero, if the vendor's model has built-in protections
explain: When anyone can inject content into the context, the attacker needs neither an account nor special knowledge. That is why likelihood is treated as high, and controls are chosen based on impact. Vendor protections reduce the risk but don't eliminate it.

q: An agent uses long-term memory and combines data from the HR and finance systems to answer managers. Which additional perspective is most useful alongside STRIDE?
options: Only checking latency
Privacy questions (e.g., LINDDUN): purpose, data linking, retention, transparency
A model accuracy benchmark
Checking library licenses
explain: STRIDE reduces leakage to a single letter. When an agent links personal data from multiple sources and remembers it, questions about purpose, linking, retention and transparency reveal risks that STRIDE doesn't highlight.

q: A chatbot without tools or RAG, with public access. Which threats take priority in the model?
options: Tool misuse and agent privilege escalation
RAG corpus poisoning
Forged messages between agents
Improper output handling, system prompt leakage, jailbreak and unbounded consumption
explain: Without tools, RAG or multiple agents, boundaries A and B remain: output that gets rendered, a prompt that can leak, attempts to bypass restrictions and the cost of public access. The other threats require components the system doesn't have.

q: Order the threat modeling activities according to the “four questions” approach.
options: Decide on controls, owners and deadlines, or accept the risk
Use tests and red teaming to verify that controls work, and update the model
Draw a DFD with AI trust boundaries and assets
Go through STRIDE, OWASP and ATLAS by elements and boundaries
explain: What are we working on (DFD) → what can go wrong (STRIDE/OWASP/ATLAS) → what are we going to do (controls) → did we do a good job (verification and update).

q: An agent that summarizes public news publishes summaries to a public channel. It has no access to internal data. How does the Rule of Two assess it?
options: It has A (untrusted input) and C (external communication), but not B, so under this rule it is acceptable without additional oversight
It has all three properties and must have confirmation for every post
The rule does not apply to public data
It has only B, so it is completely risk-free
explain: Without access to sensitive data (B), the agent has two of the three properties. That doesn't mean zero risk (e.g., reputational harm), but under the rule mandatory oversight of every action is not required.

q: Who should take part in a threat modeling workshop for a RAG assistant over documents containing personal data?
options: Only SecOps, to keep the process fast
Only the model vendor
The product owner, the orchestrator developer, someone who knows the data, SecOps and, when needed, the DPO/a lawyer
Only the data science team
explain: A threat model requires knowledge of the product, the code, the data and security; when personal data is involved, also of legal obligations. No single team sees all the flows and decisions on its own.
